entities.name: Our Lady of the Assumption Cathedral, Granada
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
Granada Cathedral (Cathedral of the Incarnation / Catedral de la Encarnación, also known as Cathedral of the Assumption of Granada) in Granada, Andalusia, Spain — begun in 1523 CE on the site of the Great Mosque of Granada immediately after the Reconquista — is the first Renaissance cathedral built in Spain and one of the most historically charged religious buildings in the country, symbolizing the Spanish Catholic reconquest of the last Muslim kingdom on Iberian soil.

The cathedral was begun by Diego de Siloé (1528) who transformed an original Gothic design into the first Spanish Renaissance cathedral, creating a revolutionary new form — the capilla mayor (main chapel) as a massive circular rotunda surrounded by classical columns — that became the prototype for subsequent Spanish Renaissance churches. The circular capilla mayor is considered one of the supreme innovations of Spanish Renaissance architecture, anticipating Roman High Renaissance circular designs.

Granada Cathedral's Royal Chapel (adjacent, technically separate) contains the tombs of Ferdinand and Isabella (Los Reyes Católicos) — the monarchs who completed the Reconquista (1492), expelled the Jews (1492), sponsored Columbus's voyage (1492), and established the Spanish Inquisition. The Royal Chapel with its effigies and the treasure of Queen Isabella (including her personal crown, scepter, and paintings) is the most historically charged royal burial chapel in Spain. The cathedral-mosque juxtaposition in Granada — the mosque's former minaret visible in the Giralda of Seville across Andalusia — makes it one of the most politically resonant sacred sites in Western history.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Granada Cathedral — Spain's first Renaissance cathedral, built on the Great Mosque site as the supreme Reconquista victory symbol, adjacent to the tombs of Ferdinand and Isabella, and containing one of the most revolutionary spatial innovations in Spanish architecture — is one of the most historically charged sacred monuments in Western history.
